excerpt: The Systematic Reviews workflow provides step-by-step guidance through search, screening, and data extraction, culminating in a research report summarizing the relevant papers.
Every Research Agent session runs at an effort level, which you set from the slider in the prompt box before you send your question.
Turn on **Instant email alerts** to be immediately alerted whenever a new relevant research paper is found.
Import from Zotero
Your Elicit Library can be exported as a .ris file, which you can import into Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote, or another reference manager.
API access
Projects in Elicit allow you to link together multiple sessions for fluid reasoning across different aspects of your work.
A skill is a set of instructions you can hand to Elicit's agent so it approaches a task a particular way.
Collaborators with edit access can ask the agent questions in your session, produce new artifacts (documents, tables, etc.), and edit other artifacts
The extension uses your active logins in your browser to download papers you can access via your institution.
To add a column, simply tell the research agent what column(s) you'd like to add. For example, you can say: "Add a column for study type."
the Research Agent can pull from a wide range of sources (e.g. publications, public filings, press releases), produce flexible outputs, and let you iterate until you have exactly what you need
click it to open the slider and move between Fastest, Fast, Balanced, Smart, and Smartest
Elicit will automatically fetch papers during the data extraction phase of your Systematic Reviews
Alerts allow you to stay up to date on the latest research about topics that are relevant to you, so you can add them to your Library for future use.
Instead of writing out the same detailed prompt every time you run a market sizing or a landscape review, you reference the skill and the agent follows it.
Invite your team members to collaborate live with you in Research Agent sessions.
Create a column for each data point you'd like to extract from your papers. Columns can pull data from the papers' body text or from tables in the papers.
Pro, Scale, and Enterprise subscribers can export tables from Systematic Reviews, including the screening recommendation tables and the data extraction table.
With Elicit's semantic search engine, you can ask a question in natural language, and Elicit will find relevant papers, without you having to think of every possible keyword to search for.
you can filter and export your sources, generate figures, and draft slides, all without leaving the conversation
Elicit supports the major steps of a systematic review: 1. Set up your review on the Setup page 2. Gather all papers for the systematic review 3. Screen papers by title and abstract
A skill is a set of instructions you can hand to Elicit's agent so it approaches a task a particular way
you can spend less time downloading full-text PDFs from publisher websites to extract in Elicit – we'll get the papers for you
Tables can be exported in CSV and Excel format. Certain tables of sources can be exported as RIS or BIB files.
Turn on Instant email alerts to be immediately alerted whenever a new relevant research paper is found.
Elicit's semantic search means you don't have to know all the right keywords to get relevant results.

I asked about media bias detection and used the topic analysis feature. A minute or so later, I had a list of concepts with citations and links to papers I can look at further. This feels like an amazing tool to do literature overviews.

Elicit states: 'assume that around 90% of the information you see in Elicit is accurate... it's very important for you to check the work in Elicit closely.' Commenter: 1/10 answers being wrong just is not good enough for a whole lot of people.
I gave it a topic I researched in depth recently. It gave me mostly incorrect summaries (one said hypothesis X is confirmed; nope it hasn't), missed key papers, dug up obscure and irrelevant ones.
It seems like it should hallucinate less, as it directly quotes, but nope, it still hallucinates just as much and then gives a quote that directly contradicts its statement.
Testing Elicit gave me quite a bit worse results than using PaperQA by futurehouse. While paperqa could understand a bit of the nuance of a scientific query, elicit did not.
LaTeX syntax being presented raw in search results, e.g. '$${\text{O}}\bigl(f\bigr)$$O(f) rounds' appeared in 'Most Relevant Sentence' on favorites page.

I tried abstract summarization with a whitepaper and it came up with completely made-up facts, describing an algorithm acronym incorrectly. I would suggest tuning this feature to be a bit less creative.

I also second the earlier complaint that the follow-up email is spam. I unsubscribed and reported it as such. I never signed up for this and was never warned I would sign up or given the option not to.
The 'Positive reframe' task setting is fun: 'Don't stab me with that knife' --> 'There are lots of ways that person can hurt me other than by stabbing me with a knife'
